lesson.title: Turning a Research Question into H0 and Ha
lesson.summary: Writing correct hypotheses means identifying the population parameter, expressing the no-difference claim as H0, and expressing the researcher's suspicion as a matching, correctly directed Ha.
lesson.body:
Translating a research question into symbols is a skill with its own common mistakes, worth practicing deliberately. The process has three steps. First, identify the population parameter of interest and define it clearly in words, using standard notation, p for a single population proportion, or p1 and p2 (or the difference p1 minus p2) for two groups being compared. Second, identify the status-quo or no-difference value for that parameter, this becomes H0, always written with an equals sign. Third, identify the direction, if any, implied by the research question, this becomes Ha, written with greater than, less than, or not equal to.

The single most common mistake is writing hypotheses about the sample statistic, p-hat, instead of the population parameter, p. This is a real error, not just a notational preference: hypotheses are always claims about the unknown population parameter, because the sample statistic is already known exactly once the data are collected, there is nothing left to test about a number you can simply calculate. A hypothesis such as 'p-hat = 0.5' does not make sense as a test, since p-hat was already computed from the sample and either equals 0.5 or it does not. Another frequent error is choosing an inequality direction in Ha that does not actually match the research question, or forgetting that H0 must contain the equals sign, never a strict inequality.

Worked example: a cereal company claims that 20 percent of its boxes contain a prize. A consumer advocacy group suspects the real proportion is lower than advertised. Let p represent the true proportion of all boxes that contain a prize. The status-quo, no-difference claim is H0: p = 0.20. The consumer group's suspicion, that the real value is lower, is directional, giving Ha: p less than 0.20.

A second example without a specified direction: a company wants to know whether redesigning its website changed the historical 8 percent conversion rate, with no reason to predict an increase or a decrease, just curiosity about whether anything changed at all. Here H0: p = 0.08 and Ha: p not equal to 0.08. A third example connects back to the two-proportion tools from earlier in this unit: testing whether two medical treatments have different true recovery rates, with p1 and p2 defined as the true recovery proportions for treatments 1 and 2, gives H0: p1 = p2 and, absent a specific predicted direction, Ha: p1 not equal to p2. Getting comfortable with this translation step matters because every later step of a hypothesis test, the test statistic, the p-value, and the conclusion, is built directly on top of however H0 and Ha were written down first.
